cards.back: To shorten a text or speech without losing the essential meaning. Example: 'The publisher released an abridged version of the novel for younger readers.'
To publicly recommend or support a particular cause or policy. Example: 'The senator advocated for increased funding for public education.'
Open to more than one interpretation; not having a clear meaning. Example: 'The ambiguous wording of the contract led to a lengthy legal dispute.'
To make a bad or unsatisfactory situation better. Example: 'The new policy was designed to ameliorate the effects of poverty on rural communities.'
Comparable in certain respects, typically in a way that makes something clearer. Example: 'The professor explained that the structure of an atom is analogous to a solar system.'
A short, interesting story about a real incident or person, often used to illustrate a point. Example: 'The author opened the essay with an anecdote about her grandmother to humanize the topic.'
To support, strengthen, or reinforce something. Example: 'New archaeological discoveries bolstered the historian's controversial thesis.'
Truthful and straightforward; frank in expression. Example: 'The journalist's candid reporting revealed the true conditions inside the factory.'
To find a way around an obstacle or to overcome a problem cleverly. Example: 'The students tried to circumvent the restrictions by submitting their papers through a different portal.'
Showing smug or uncritical satisfaction with oneself or one's achievements. Example: 'The editorial warned citizens against becoming complacent about threats to democratic institutions.'
To admit that something is true after first resisting or denying it. Example: 'The researcher conceded that the sample size was too small to draw definitive conclusions.'
An opinion or conclusion formed on the basis of incomplete information. Example: 'Without sufficient evidence, the historian's claim remained mere conjecture.'
To come together from different directions to meet at a single point. Example: 'Several lines of evidence converge to support the theory of plate tectonics.'
To confirm or give support to a statement, theory, or finding. Example: 'Witness testimony corroborated the evidence presented by the forensic team.'
Able to be believed or trusted as reliable. Example: 'The journalist verified the claims with three credible sources before publishing the story.'
To reduce in extent or quantity; to impose a restriction on. Example: 'Budget cuts forced the university to curtail its study-abroad programs.'
Humble submission and respect shown toward another person. Example: 'The young scholar spoke with deference when addressing the distinguished professor.'
Done consciously and intentionally; carefully considered. Example: 'The author's deliberate use of repetition reinforces the central theme of the passage.'
To publicly declare something to be wrong or evil. Example: 'The editorial denounced the proposed legislation as a threat to civil liberties.'
To use up the supply or resources of something. Example: 'Excessive groundwater pumping has depleted aquifers across the Great Plains.'
To perceive or recognize something that is not immediately obvious. Example: 'Experienced readers can discern the author's bias even in seemingly objective reporting.'
A person's inherent qualities of mind and character; a tendency or inclination. Example: 'Her cheerful disposition made her well-suited to working with young students.'
Tending to be different or to develop in different directions. Example: 'The two scholars offered divergent interpretations of the same historical document.'
To draw out a response, answer, or reaction from someone. Example: 'The interviewer's probing questions elicited revealing answers from the candidate.'
Fluent, persuasive, and expressive in speaking or writing. Example: 'Frederick Douglass was known for his eloquent speeches against the institution of slavery.'
To give a tangible or visible form to an idea, quality, or feeling. Example: 'The constitution embodies the principles of equality and justice.'
To match or surpass someone by imitation. Example: 'Aspiring writers often emulate the style of authors they admire.'
Not even or regular in pattern or movement; unpredictable. Example: 'The patient's erratic heartbeat prompted doctors to order additional tests.'
To make a problem, bad situation, or negative feeling worse. Example: 'The drought exacerbated food shortages in communities already facing economic hardship.'
To serve as a typical example of something. Example: 'The case study exemplifies the challenges that arise when public health policy conflicts with individual rights.'
Possible and practical to accomplish. Example: 'The committee determined that constructing a new library on campus was financially feasible.'
Incapable of producing any useful result; pointless. Example: 'Attempts to negotiate a ceasefire proved futile as both sides refused to compromise.'
To shock or excite someone into taking action. Example: 'The tragic event galvanized the community into demanding stricter safety regulations.'
Treating all people and groups equally; not biased. Example: 'A fair trial requires an impartial jury that can evaluate evidence without prejudice.'
To delay or prevent something by obstructing it. Example: 'Lack of access to reliable internet impedes educational opportunities in remote areas.'
Marking the beginning of an institution, activity, or period of office. Example: 'The professor delivered the inaugural lecture for the new environmental studies program.'
Expressed clearly and easy to understand. Example: 'The textbook's lucid explanations made complex scientific concepts accessible to beginners.'
To make something less severe, serious, or painful. Example: 'Engineers designed the seawall to mitigate the impact of storm surges on coastal towns.'
A subtle difference in meaning, expression, or sound. Example: 'The essay demonstrated an appreciation for the nuances of the author's argument.'
A statement or situation that seems contradictory but may reveal a deeper truth. Example: 'The paradox of choice suggests that having too many options can lead to less satisfaction.'
Dealing with things sensibly and realistically based on practical considerations. Example: 'The committee adopted a pragmatic approach to solving the budget crisis.'
To prevent something from happening; to make impossible. Example: 'The lack of funding precluded the team from conducting a second round of experiments.'
To prove a statement or theory to be wrong or false. Example: 'The new data effectively refuted the long-held assumption about the age of the fossil.'
The art of effective or persuasive speaking or writing. Example: 'The candidate's powerful rhetoric inspired thousands of voters to support the initiative.'
To examine or inspect closely and thoroughly. Example: 'Peer reviewers scrutinized the methodology before the paper was accepted for publication.'
Not easily convinced; having doubts or reservations. Example: 'Many scientists remained skeptical of the findings until they were independently verified.'
To provide evidence to support or prove the truth of something. Example: 'The lawyer presented documents to substantiate her client's alibi.'
To weaken or damage something gradually or insidiously. Example: 'Spreading misinformation can undermine public trust in scientific institutions.'
To clear someone of blame or suspicion; to show that something is justified. Example: 'The discovery of new evidence vindicated the researcher whose theory had been dismissed for years.'
Feeling or showing caution about possible dangers or problems. Example: 'Historians are wary of relying on a single primary source when reconstructing past events.'
